guidance: ACL reading only: it explains the entries you paste and the mask that governs them. It is not a chmod or umask converter, it does not read or change any file, and it takes no view on whether the rights it shows are the ones you should grant.
method: Entries follow the acl(5) text form: an optional default: prefix, then a tag (user/u, group/g, mask/m, other/o), an optional qualifier and a permissions field. Permissions may be written as r, w and x in any order with dashes ignored, or as a single octal digit, and they become the three-bit value r=4, w=2, x=1. Comments from a hash to the end of the line are stripped, which makes getfacl output paste directly, including its #effective: notes. Validity follows acl(5) and setfacl(1): exactly one u::, one g:: and one o::, at most one m::, no duplicate qualifier for a named user or group, and a default ACL that, when any default entry is present, repeats those three base entries and carries its own mask when it names a user or group. Default entries are refused unless the object is marked as a directory. When a mask entry exists it is the ceiling: the effective rights of g::, every named user and every named group are the granted bits AND the mask, while u:: and o:: are never masked. When named entries exist and no mask was written, the mask is what setfacl would add - the union of g:: and every named user and group - and it is reported as added rather than given. The mode ls -l prints comes from u::, the mask (or g:: when there is no mask) and o::, because acl(5) maps the group permission bits onto the mask; a + follows the mode when the ACL goes beyond the three base entries or a default ACL exists. The canonical short form always writes the mask explicitly, which keeps setfacl from recalculating it. Input is up to 32 entries and every refusal names the line and the entry. It reads no file, runs no command, and keeps no record.
